common_name: I'll Take Manhattan Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Ruffled Pink Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Keith Keppel introduced this heavily ruffled white-and-fuchsia plicata in 2010, and it won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2016.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface uncovered in gritty, sharply drained soil, since this cultivar's heavy ruffling comes from vigorous, thick-textured falls that rot quickly if the crown stays wet. I'll Take Manhattan carries a white ground stitched and washed in bright fuchsia-pink around the edges of both standards and falls, a stippled plicata pattern crisp enough to have earned Keppel's introduction the Dykes Medal within six years of release. Feed lightly with a low-nitrogen fertilizer after bloom to encourage strong rhizome increase without inviting rot. Divide congested clumps every three to four years, replanting only firm, disease-free fans.

common_name: Feature Attraction Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Cream-and-Wine Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; Schreiner's Gardens introduced this cream-ground plicata and it won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1998.

directions: Plant rhizomes with the top surface exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, since this vigorous Schreiner introduction is prone to rot in heavy, waterlogged clay. Feature Attraction shows a soft cream-to-ivory ground brushed and stippled with wine-red-violet around the hafts and edges, a refined plicata pattern that earned it the Dykes Medal a few years after its release. Its tall, well-branched stalks carry many buds in succession, making it a reliable choice for a long bloom display in a mixed perennial border. Lift and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after flowering to keep bloom count high.

common_name: Romantic Evening Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Deep Red-Violet Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; this deep red-violet Schreiner's Gardens self won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2003.

directions: Set rhizomes just below the soil surface with the top exposed to full sun in sharply drained ground, since this iris's dense flower substance shows best where roots never sit wet. Romantic Evening carries velvety, deep red-violet standards and falls of near-uniform color, a saturated self so richly toned that its blooms can read almost black-purple in low afternoon light. The heavy ruffling and broad falls place it among the most photographed of Schreiner's dark-toned Dykes Medal winners, and it pairs well against pale yellow or white companions in a border. Divide every three to four years after bloom, discarding the oldest center rhizomes to keep new growth vigorous.

common_name: Point Well Taken Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal White-and-Purple Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; this Schreiner's Gardens bitone won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 2013.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally with the top surface uncovered in well-drained soil, giving this heavy-substanced bitone plenty of air movement around the crown to discourage rot. Point Well Taken pairs crisp white standards with deep violet-purple falls edged in a matching band, a bold two-tone contrast carried on tall, sturdy, well-branched stalks. The strong color break between standards and falls makes it a striking focal point when massed at the back of a sunny perennial bed. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom finishes to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Blue Shimmer Bearded Iris (Historic 1927 Blue-Stitched Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Grace Sturtevant registered this white-ground plicata in 1927, and it remains a widely grown heirloom nearly a century later.

directions: Set rhizomes with the top surface exposed to full sun in lean, sharply drained soil; older heirloom cultivars like this one tend to rot quickly if planted too deep or kept consistently moist. Blue Shimmer bears a white ground finely streaked and dashed with soft blue-violet through the center of each fall, a delicate broken-color pattern that was considered strikingly modern when Grace Sturtevant introduced it in the late 1920s. Nearly a century of continuous commercial availability has made it a benchmark heirloom for gardeners assembling a historic iris collection alongside newer ruffled hybrids. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Ambassadeur Bearded Iris (Historic 1920 French Bronze-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; the Cayeux family of France introduced this smoky bronze-and-violet bicolor in 1920, one of the influential early-twentieth-century imports that reshaped American iris breeding.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, following the same shallow-planting rule that suits all tall bearded iris. Ambassadeur pairs coppery bronze standards with rich red-violet falls, a smoky, saturated bicolor blend that was prized in French gardens of the 1920s and widely exported to American collections during the interwar golden age of iris breeding. Its deep, warm coloring makes it a good companion for the paler heirloom plicatas and blue selfs of the same era in a period border. Divide every three to four years after bloom, since older French heirlooms of this vintage tend to lose vigor if left undivided too long.
sources: Societe Francaise des Iris et Plantes Bulbeuses

common_name: Depute Nomblot Bearded Iris (Historic 1929 Coppery Bronze French Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; the Cayeux firm of Orleans, France registered this coppery bronze-red self in 1929.

directions: Set rhizomes with the top surface uncovered in sharply drained soil, since this early French cultivar's compact stature and modest substance make it more susceptible to rot in wet clay than modern hybrids. Depute Nomblot carries a warm coppery bronze-red tone across both standards and falls, a self color that was among the deepest available in French iris breeding of the late 1920s. It is a good choice for gardeners recreating an authentic period planting of interwar-era French and American tall bearded introductions. Divide every three to four years after bloom to maintain steady flowering, as this heirloom's rhizomes multiply more slowly than modern ramped-up hybrids.
sources: Societe Francaise des Iris et Plantes Bulbeuses

common_name: Gracchus Bearded Iris (Historic 1884 Yellow Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; John Salter of England registered this yellow-ground plicata in 1884, making it one of the oldest tall bearded cultivars still in commercial circulation.

directions: Plant rhizomes with the top surface exposed to full sun in lean, well-drained soil, since this nineteenth-century cultivar predates modern breeding for rot resistance and does best left undisturbed once established. Gracchus displays a pale yellow ground heavily veined and stitched with reddish-brown around the falls, an antique plicata pattern that has been continuously grown by heirloom iris collectors since Victorian times. Its shorter stature and smaller flowers compared with modern tall bearded hybrids reflect its nineteenth-century origin, making it a useful reference point for the earliest era of named iris cultivars. Leave clumps undivided for several years, since flowering can be sparse the season immediately after transplanting.

common_name: Jean Cayeux Bearded Iris (Historic 1931 French Tan-and-Violet Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; the Cayeux family of Orleans, France introduced this warm tan-and-violet blend in 1931, naming it for a family member.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, giving the crown room to bake dry between waterings as it would in the Loire Valley nurseries where it originated. Jean Cayeux blends warm tan-brown standards with falls flushed in soft reddish-violet, an unusual smoky color combination that distinguished it from the cooler blues and purples common in iris breeding of its era. As one of the enduring Cayeux family introductions of the early 1930s, it remains sought after by collectors building a historic French iris collection. Divide every three to four years after bloom to keep clumps vigorous and free-flowering.
sources: Societe Francaise des Iris et Plantes Bulbeuses

common_name: Indian Chief Bearded Iris (Historic 1929 Sass Coppery-Red Blend Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun; Nebraska hybridizer Hans Sass registered this coppery rose-red blend in 1929, part of the Sass family's influential push toward warmer iris tones.

directions: Plant rhizomes with the top surface uncovered in sharply drained soil, since older Sass-era cultivars are less tolerant of soggy crowns than modern hybrids bred for garden vigor. Indian Chief carries a warm coppery rose-red blend across both standards and falls, one of the deeper, warmer tones the Sass brothers pursued as they moved American iris breeding away from the blues and violets that had dominated earlier decades. It remains a useful marker of the transitional 1920s breeding period when hybridizers first began chasing red and copper tones in tall bearded iris. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to sustain good flowering.

common_name: Autumn Circus Bearded Iris (Historic 1948 Tan-and-White Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top exposed, in late summer to early fall; Schreiner's Gardens introduced this tan-and-white plicata in the late 1940s, and it became one of the best-known blend patterns of its era.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, allowing the crown to dry between waterings. Autumn Circus pairs buff-tan standards with white falls stitched and dotted in maroon-red around the edges, a warm-toned plicata pattern that stood out among the cooler blues and purples common in mid-century iris breeding. Its distinctive tan-and-maroon combination made it a popular parent for later plicata breeding lines, and named seedlings tracing back to this cross still turn up in modern iris pedigrees. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep flowering strong.
